stories.headline: Goldman Sachs pulls Claude Code from its traders and bankers, keeping it for engineers
stories.why_read: The bank that praised trader-built "vibe coding" tools in July has now drawn the line at role. If you're writing the agent policy for a big enterprise, this is the template everyone will be quoting.
body: Internal guidance updated in October restricts Anthropic's Claude Code and Microsoft's GitHub tools to Goldman's engineers, Bloomberg reported, after a review of productivity and risk. Strats who straddle trading, quant research, and engineering keep access, but most traders and bankers lost it. They had been using the agents to monitor client flows, model positions, and assemble written and graphic material. Goldman's in-house assistant, which uses models from several vendors, is still available firm-wide; the restriction targets third-party agents that write and run code on their own.

The reasoning is the interesting part: a coding agent typically runs with the same access as the person using it, on the same machine that handles client data, and code a banker generates never passes through the review an engineer's would. The irony is hard to miss. Goldman and Morgan Stanley are lead underwriters on Anthropic's IPO, so for the next few weeks Goldman's bankers will be marketing shares in a company whose flagship agent most of them can't use.

stories.headline: Starship Flight 15 is set for November 13 with a try at catching both booster and ship
stories.why_read: If both catches work, SpaceX recovers an entire orbital rocket for the first time. That's the moment rapid reuse stops being a slide and starts being a schedule.
body: SpaceX is targeting a 75-minute window opening at 4:45 p.m. CT on Thursday, November 13 from Starbase. The plan is a Super Heavy catch a little over six minutes after liftoff, then a ship catch at the tower after roughly 22 hours and about 14 orbits at around 275 km. Along the way the ship deploys 26 Starlink V3 satellites, three of them carrying cameras aimed at the heat shield.

The vehicle flies with upgraded tiles and flaps, and the upper-stage catch only goes ahead after strict safety checks on the way down. Elon Musk calls it a critical step toward rapid reuse, and for a Texan watching from Austin it's a short drive from being a spectator sport.

stories.headline: Terafab tells suppliers it wants 1 million wafers a month from 2032
stories.why_read: That number would put a Tesla-SpaceX fab in the same league as the biggest chipmakers on Earth. It's the clearest signal yet of how much silicon Musk thinks robots, Cybercabs, and orbital compute will eat.
body: Nikkei reports that Terafab, the joint Tesla-SpaceX semiconductor plant in Grimes County, Texas, has told equipment suppliers it is targeting 1 million wafers per month from 2032 onward: 700,000 for memory and 300,000 for logic. The post Anand reposted put the reaction in one word, and the memory split is what jumped out to most chip watchers.

The project starts with a $16.8 billion investment on a former power-plant site, and satellite images show construction underway. The stated customers are internal: Optimus robots, Cybercab, and SpaceX's space-based data centers. Skeptics point out that a fab's capacity on paper and its yield in practice are different animals, so the supplier orders over the next two years are the thing to watch.

stories.headline: SpaceX plans a $24 billion AI supercomputer and its own power plant at Starbase
stories.why_read: SpaceX is building compute and generation side by side so it doesn't have to wait on the Texas grid. That pattern, bring your own power, is quickly becoming the default for AI campuses.
body: The project covers 444 acres near Brownsville, with up to 35 gas turbines providing 748 megawatts for the supercomputer. SpaceX would own and run both the computer and the plant, construction is already underway, and a public hearing on tax incentives is set for December 9.

It lands the same week SpaceX pitched its much larger Arizona campus, and the same weekend Anthropic's gas-generator purchase made headlines. Supporters see a clever end run around interconnection queues tied directly to Starship operations; critics will be at that December hearing asking about emissions and the incentives.

stories.headline: Did Opus 5.5 get nerfed on November 3, or just its summarizer?
stories.why_read: Heavy Claude users noticed its visible reasoning changed overnight. Whether the model got worse or only the display did matters a lot if you're paying for high-effort runs.
body: A widely shared post says Claude Opus 5.5's thinking patterns shifted on November 3, and the Hacker News thread filled up fast with people who felt it too. Several said they had to bump their default reasoning level to get the old behavior back, and one compared the drop to sliding back to an older DeepSeek.

Others in the thread argue the change is only a new summarizer for the reasoning trace, with the model itself unchanged, and some say things have already improved. Speculation runs to a new model arriving around Qwen4's expected drop and Anthropic's IPO. Without an official note it's unproven either way, which is exactly why teams that depend on one model want their own regression evals.

stories.headline: Researchers chained web bugs to unlock an automaker's cars from just a plate number
stories.why_read: No hardware hacking at all: an exposed admin tool, a WAF gap, and an MFA skip. It's a vivid reminder that the car's real attack surface is its cloud backend.
body: Shubham Shah and Sam Curry looked at a major automaker's connected-car platform starting from one question: what does the app talk to when you remotely unlock? That led to an admin test harness on the public internet, OpenIDM admin credentials sitting in a JavaScript vendor bundle, and a path-traversal trick to slip past the WAF. Notably, the winning bypass prefix came from letting GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra grind on it for about six hours after the humans had given up on that angle.

From there they could reset any user's password, skip multi-factor through a password-grant OAuth flow, mint a mobile app token, and call the remote command API. The final chain went plate to VIN to subscriber to car, and the combined write-ups cover remote unlock and engine start across Australia, the US, and Canada. They tested only on cars they owned or had permission to use.

stories.headline: Outlook.com is quietly bouncing mail from domains without a DMARC record
stories.why_read: This one hits small senders, not just bulk mailers, and nobody announced it. The fix is a single DNS TXT record you can add this morning.
body: Since November 5, Microsoft's consumer mail service (outlook.com, hotmail.com, live.com, msn.com) has been rejecting some messages from domains that publish no DMARC record, according to MailRoute. The domains it saw bounced mostly had working SPF and often DKIM; what they lacked was the DMARC record tying those to the From address. Only some messages bounce, so "my mail is getting through" isn't proof you're fine.

This differs from Microsoft's published May 2025 rule for senders of more than 5,000 messages a day: it reaches one-line replies from small offices, and as of November 6 there was no postmaster notice or blog post. The suggested fix is v=DMARC1; p=none, which changes nothing about how other receivers treat your mail but gets you past the check.

stories.headline: Tesla adds 38 Model Ys and its Texas Robotaxi fleet hits 1,282
stories.why_read: The tracker Anand follows says Tesla is now within a handful of Waymo's Texas robotaxi registrations. The fleet count is becoming the scoreboard.
body: The Texas Autonomous Vehicle Tracker reported that Tesla Robotaxi just added 38 Model Ys, bringing its Texas fleet to 1,282 vehicles. A follow-up post Anand also reposted says that leaves Tesla four vehicles short of Waymo in robotaxis registered in Texas.

The same poster flagged something odd: plenty of new Model Y registrations but few new Cybercab ones. With Tesla saying the next Cybercab will run on a smaller pack, the mix between the two is worth watching as the fleet grows.

stories.headline: Herb Sutter on why the C++26 ballot failed: the creator and the committee disagreed
stories.why_read: A rare inside account of standards governance breaking down over contracts. If you rely on C++, this decides what C++26 ships and when.
body: In WG21 paper P4454R0, Herb Sutter argues that the C++26 Draft International Standard ballot failed for one decisive reason: Bjarne Stroustrup strongly disagreed with the committee's consensus on contracts, and the national bodies chose to give his view more weight. The vote in Croydon in March was 114 in favor of C++26 with contracts and 12 against.

Sutter lays out the grievances on both sides without trying to settle who's right, notes that C++ has dropped features before (export, concepts, exception specifications, contracts in C++20) but always with Bjarne's assent before a DIS vote, and looks at how other languages survived similar splits before sketching options for getting C++26 out the door.

stories.headline: ChatGPT Desktop forwards your SSH agent to remote machines
stories.why_read: A remote agent that borrows your local SSH keys can push to your private repos. Worth checking before you point it at a shared box.
body: An HN post points to a Codex pull request discussion showing that an agent on a remote machine can authenticate with your local SSH credentials through agent forwarding, which means it could, for example, push to your private GitHub repositories.

The top suggestion in the thread is keeping SSH keys in the macOS Secure Enclave with a fingerprint required for each new session, so an agent can't start a connection silently. Another commenter put the broader point well: in security, friction is a feature, and removing it for convenience is how surprises happen.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang apologizes to Nvidia staff and the board opens an independent investigation
stories.why_read: The CEO of the company behind most AI compute wrote a personal letter, and it mentions national security concerns. That last part is what investors and partners will track.
body: In a message posted to Nvidia's newsroom, Jensen Huang apologized to his family and to employees, writing that he was unfaithful to his wife and takes full responsibility. He said he remains fully committed to Nvidia and will work to earn back colleagues' and shareholders' confidence, and asked for privacy for his family.

The letter also says Nvidia's board has started an independent investigation into the national security concerns raised in news reports, and that Huang will cooperate fully. The HN thread is enormous; the business question is how long the investigation runs and what it covers.

stories.headline: Nvidia was in 1 of every 11 startup rounds over $100 million last year
stories.why_read: Nvidia out-invested every venture firm except Sequoia and a16z in big rounds, and that's before counting its venture arm. Its customers are increasingly its portfolio.
body: Data Hyena counted 903 venture rounds of $100 million or more between October 2025 and September 2026 that named investors. Nvidia or NVentures was in 79 of them, more than Sequoia (75) or Andreessen Horowitz (73), and Nvidia on its own was in 65, ahead of Lightspeed, General Catalyst, and Accel.

Its rounds ranged from Reflection AI and Baseten to Nscale and PhysicsX. Corporates showed up in 38% of big rounds, up from 35% a year earlier, with Salesforce (32), GV (29), and AMD (16) trailing well behind Nvidia.

stories.headline: A contrarian case that the AI bubble may not be a bubble
stories.why_read: Almost every thread assumes the pop is coming. This argues the spending is mostly one-time buildout, and the comments push back hard, which makes it a good stress test of your own view.
body: Matteo Raso starts from the scale: at least $3 trillion in committed spending and an estimated $1.9 trillion already spent. He concedes the financing vehicles make the real exposure hard to see, which he calls one of the strongest points for the bubble case.

His core claim is that data center construction is a one-off capital cost, not an ongoing expense, so spending should fall sharply once the buildout is done. With nearly 600 comments, the HN discussion is a useful map of the counterarguments, from depreciation of GPUs to who ends up holding the debt.

stories.headline: Tests suggest the coding harness matters as much as the model
stories.why_read: Same model, different scaffolding, double-digit swings. If you're choosing between Cursor, Claude Code, and friends, this is the variable most comparisons ignore.
body: Garry Tan ran seven harnesses on the same 20 coding tasks and saw scores from 71% to 79%, though 14 tasks came out identical everywhere. A separate study of eleven production systems, including Claude Code and OpenHands, mapped seven core subsystems and found harnesses have grown into full platforms by mid-2026.

On Terminal-Bench 2.0, the same model across nine harnesses varied by a wide margin. Taken with MaxxBench's findings, the message is that benchmark numbers describe a model-plus-harness pair, not a model.

stories.headline: Greg Brockman says frontier models with heavy test-time compute are becoming discovery engines
stories.why_read: OpenAI is pointing at a claimed Navier-Stokes proof checked in Lean. Treat it as a claim until mathematicians weigh in, but it's the kind of claim that changes the conversation.
body: Brockman highlighted an OpenAI effort in which thousands of AI agents worked for 88 hours to produce a proof related to the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize Problem, verified in the Lean proof assistant, according to the X summary of the discussion. Google DeepMind's Pushmeet Kohli described a phase transition in his lab's discovery pace, with new releases coming soon.

It's landing in the middle of a separate X argument where a skeptic challenged people to name one major LLM achievement; replies pointed to OpenAI's wave of more than 700 math papers with verified proofs and a full AI translation of China's Twenty-Four Histories. Independent review of the proof is the thing to wait for.

stories.headline: METR finds Anthropic's progress has doubled in pace since late 2025
stories.why_read: Most of the speedup is attributed to AI helping the researchers. That's the recursive loop forecasters have been watching for, showing up in a measurement.
body: A METR assessment covering August to October 2026 shows Anthropic's capability gains on key benchmarks running about twice as fast as before October 2025, with roughly 80% of the speedup credited to AI assisting researchers.

Anthropic also rolled out a four-layer memory system of transcripts, self-written notes, linked wikis, and a "dreaming" consolidation step. It lifted a database task score from 0.655 to 0.838 and wiki accuracy from 13% to 48%. The curves are running ahead of the 2027 forecasts many people were using.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang tells US companies to use Chinese open models, and the internet makes memes
stories.why_read: Nvidia's CEO is publicly pushing Kimi, DeepSeek, and GLM. For open-weights fans that's a notable endorsement, whatever the jokes say.
body: In an Axios interview, Huang urged US companies to adopt open-source Chinese models like Kimi, DeepSeek, and GLM, arguing they widen access to AI and drive demand for Nvidia hardware.

A short clip resurfaced this weekend and turned into a meme about which kind of "Chinese models" he meant, with the joke posts racking up thousands of likes. Underneath the humor is a real policy tension over open weights from China in US stacks.

stories.headline: Musk says the Grok Bot team is shipping fixes overnight
stories.why_read: He promised a dramatic improvement by the next day and asked people to reply if they still see problems. Anand reposted it, and this is the assistant running his Daily Diff.
body: Elon Musk posted that he had just done a round-table review with the Grok Bot engineering team, that fixes were being implemented overnight, and that users should notice a dramatic improvement by the next day.

He invited anyone still hitting issues to reply to the post so the team could address them right away. It's a direct line for feedback, and the replies make a handy snapshot of what users are struggling with.

stories.headline: Qualcomm and SpaceX team up on a big US 5G buildout for Starlink Mobile
stories.why_read: SpaceX building ground cell sites, not just satellites, is a direct shot at the carriers. It blends orbit and towers into one network.
body: SpaceX will build base stations for its Starlink Mobile service, with Qualcomm supplying the radio silicon and Dragonwing platforms for tens of thousands of cell sites. Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon called it one of the largest 5G deployments in the country, with an AI-native architecture.
Deployment starts in 2027. Market reaction was mixed, but the strategy is clear: combine satellite and terrestrial coverage to compete with traditional wireless carriers.

stories.headline: NASA opens astronaut applications for its permanent Moon base
stories.why_read: Applications close December 3, and the contractors are lining up. Impulse founder Tom Mueller's post on in-space transport explains why the logistics are the hard part.
body: NASA began recruiting astronauts this past weekend for work building infrastructure at the lunar south pole and preparing for Mars, open to US citizens with advanced STEM skills. It follows up to $10 billion in CLPS 2 lunar cargo contracts over ten years to companies including SpaceX, Blue Origin, and Impulse Space, plus $1.3 billion for in-space transport.

Tom Mueller, in a post Anand reposted, said Impulse won two task orders for the Moon Base program and argued an enduring lunar presence needs a whole fleet of spacecraft with different performance profiles, the way Earth needs cars, trucks, trains, and planes. Impulse is building that with its Mira, Helios, and lander vehicles.

stories.headline: Starlink customers are seeing bills climb under new demand-based pricing
stories.why_read: Some residential plans now hit $156 a month. If you're on Starlink at home, your price depends on how busy your area is.
body: Starlink users report monthly bills rising as much as $36 in a year, with some plans reaching $156 under a capacity-based model tied to local supply and demand. One customer saw a jump from $130 to $156 right after installing his dish.

Separately, standard US residential plans moved from $120 to $130, with more hikes expected under the dynamic model. The complaints come as Musk talks up moving most future AI computing to orbit for constant solar power.

stories.headline: A bipartisan Senate bill would fast-track data centers but make them pay for their own power
stories.why_read: This is the policy fight behind every new AI campus. The ratepayer-protection clause is the piece that could actually defuse local opposition.
body: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, from Senators Capito, Lee, Whitehouse, and Heinrich, would shorten environmental reviews for pipelines, mines, power plants, and AI data centers, while requiring large data centers to cover their own electricity costs. President Trump urged the Senate to pass it.

A post Anand bookmarked captures the other side of the debate: anyone who played SimCity would zone for clean, high-tax, low-traffic data centers in a heartbeat, so the resistance must be about something other than the buildings themselves.

stories.headline: Base Power wants an HQ campus next to its Austin factories
stories.why_read: A home-battery company is putting down deep roots near the airport. Austin's energy tech scene keeps growing, and this one's on Tuesday's Planning Commission agenda.
body: A zoning change for a Base Power headquarters campus goes before Austin's Planning Commission on Tuesday, November 10. The site is about 20 acres beside two Base Power manufacturing facilities under construction on Metropolis Drive near US 183 and the airport.

The change would allow buildings up to 85 feet, and the first is tentatively planned as a five-story office building. It's a local signal that home energy storage is turning into a real Austin industry.

stories.headline: An open-source SketchUp alternative built in Rust and WebGPU
stories.why_read: Free, no account, runs in the browser or on desktop, and imports SketchUp geometry. A good weekend project tool and a neat Rust-on-the-web showcase.
body: Posted to HN as KetchUp and now presented as BenchUp, the app is a free 3D modeler aimed at woodworking and furniture design. You sketch lines and rectangles, Push/Pull faces into solids, snap to geometry, type exact lengths, and organize with groups, components, and tags.
It runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, or a desktop browser, autosaves locally, saves portable .ketchup projects, imports SketchUp geometry, and exports OBJ. It's MIT-licensed and written in Rust.

stories.headline: Dux is a free, open-source desktop shell for niri, Hyprland, and Sway
stories.why_read: Tiling Wayland compositors are great until you want a polished panel, file manager, and theming. Dux bundles all of that.
body: Dux pairs a modern shell with smooth animations and widgets for media, weather, calendar, and system controls with a keyboard-first file manager that has tabs, split view, and network shares. It also includes a stateless system monitor, a greetd greeter, fast file search, and calendar sync with Google, Microsoft, CalDAV, and iCloud.

Its theming engine generates matching colors for GTK3, GTK4, Qt, terminals, and editors, including a custom 16-color palette tuned for contrast in light and dark modes. It's supported by sponsors and more than 115 Ko-fi backers.

stories.headline: Declarative dragging: say what a diagram can become, and drag-and-drop falls out
stories.why_read: Making things draggable usually means fiddly geometry code. This research flips it around, and the demos are a joy to play with.
body: Joshua Horowitz, Andrew Blinn, and Jeffrey Heer propose that instead of programming drag behavior, you declare which future states dragging an element can lead to. Their system speculatively renders those states and blends the possible worlds into a smooth, responsive interaction.

The approach is composable, with modifiers for floating, snapping, and transitions, and it ships as Dragology, a library for SVG interfaces on the web. The authors find it especially suited to explorable explanations that show the same system from several perspectives.

stories.headline: How one developer stopped drowning in 20 parallel agent sessions
stories.why_read: If juggling Claude Code and Codex tabs leaves you fried, this is a practical system: a ticket queue in git and a single inbox for decisions only you can make.
body: Sergey Kuhne describes the familiar spiral: start a task, start another while the first runs, then each reply spawns follow-ups until you're holding twenty contexts in your head. He decided the real problems were sequencing and context.

His fix keeps every ticket as a markdown file in the repo, with the board as a committed snapshot, and an agent works that board in cycles, building only tickets a human marked safe and never deploying to production. Anything needing judgment lands in one prioritized owner inbox, so nothing important lives in a chat window or in his head.

stories.headline: RIP, Harvest: a beloved invoicing tool gets a 10x price hike
stories.why_read: A clean case study in what happens to simple, focused SaaS after a private-equity-style acquisition. Freelancers in the comments share their replacements.
body: Kyle Kingsbury (aphyr) used Harvest for about a decade to track time and send invoices, and praised it as exactly what small-business software should be: focused, reliable, and reasonably priced. After Bending Spoons bought it in 2025, his price went from $13.32 to $133.98 a month.
He wrote to support and found the replies now come from a language model. The comments recommend alternatives like Cushion, Odoo, and a local-first time tracker that saves to plain text.

stories.headline: lcamtuf builds a kitchen timer with a quasi-logarithmic analog dial
stories.why_read: A delightful bit of engineering and design math: a dial that's precise for short times and still readable for long ones.
body: Annoyed by clunky appliance timers and imprecise wind-up ones, lcamtuf built a digital timer with an old-school analog display and a single adjustment knob.

A true log scale doesn't suit minutes and seconds, so he split the dial into linear sections: ten-second ticks up to one minute, minute marks from 1 to 5 minutes, five-minute marks from 5 to 30, and so on. It's the kind of small, careful build that makes you want to grab a soldering iron.

stories.headline: Nine out of every 10 time capsules go missing
stories.why_read: A charming long read for the coffee break, starting with the 1976 Bicentennial Wagon Train and what happened to the time capsules people buried.
body: Ashley Stimpson's Longreads feature opens with the Bicentennial Wagon Train, five caravans of up to 300 horse-drawn wagons that rolled toward Valley Forge for July 4, 1976, collecting signatures on rededication scrolls along the way.

From there it follows the strange afterlife of time capsules, most of which are never recovered because nobody remembers where they went. It's a gentle reminder that preserving the past takes more than burying it.
